clue.text: Sticky and wet — as shellfish?

blocks.note: first meaning: unpleasantly damp and tacky to the touch
second, whimsical meaning: like a clam, the shellfish, as 'fishy' is like a fish

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second reading as a jokey coinage: an adjective built from the name of a bivalve, the way other -y words describe likeness.
explanation.definitionFit: Damp, sweaty skin is commonly described with this adjective, and the setter also treats it as meaning resembling a bivalve.

clue.text: Full figure? Chap regularly quick to conceal it

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter of the word is kept
to conceal something is to hide it inside, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: first and third letters of the word
pacy means fast
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man is asked to hide something quickly, after a cryptic remark about a full figure.
explanation.walkthrough: CA then PACY holding IT gives CAPACITY. 'Full figure' reads like a description of a body shape, but it means the full number something can hold.
explanation.definitionFit: A venue's maximum attendance number is its capacity, so the full figure possible is that limit.

clue.text: Backs in Barcelona football game never sit on the ball

indicators.note: the back of each word is its final letter, so those tail letters are kept

blocks.note: final letters of these five words

explanation.surface: Defenders in a Barcelona football match are told never to sit down on the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backs' looks like footballing defenders, but it means the backs, or ends, of the words; 'on the ball' then switches from soccer to an idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for being quick-witted and attentive describes someone watchful and ready, which is what alert means.

clue.text: Staff will confiscate the dodgy weapon

indicators.note: something dodgy is unreliable or not straight, so these letters are scrambled
confiscating means taking something in and holding it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: a mace is a ceremonial staff
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Police staff will seize a dangerous weapon from a suspect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees, but here it is a mace, the ceremonial rod carried in parades; it surrounds a rearranged THE.
explanation.definitionFit: This broad-bladed chopping knife is used as a tool and also as a cutting arm in combat.

clue.text: Small, small nails — a lot

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
tacks are short sharp nails

explanation.surface: Tiny little nails, and plenty of them, as in a carpenter's box.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'small' looks like emphasis, but the first one is the single-letter abbreviation and the second belongs to the nails.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, having heaps or piles of something means having a great quantity of it.

clue.text: Capital E x 3, did you say?

indicators.note: asking what someone said points to the spoken form, not the spelling

blocks.note: three letter Es make a triple E, which when spoken matches the city name

explanation.surface: Someone checks whether they heard a capital letter E repeated three times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital E' looks like an upper-case letter, but 'Capital' is the definition, a city, and 'E x 3' is a triple E.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripoli is the seat of government of Libya, so it is a national capital city.

clue.text: Queen bringing two little boys into line turned up

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning something up flips it so it reads bottom to top
bringing things into a place puts them inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: an arc is a curved line
Leo and Pat, two short boys' names

explanation.surface: A queen arrives with two small boys and makes them stand in a line.
explanation.walkthrough: ARC turned upwards becomes CRA, and the pet names LEO and PAT go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleopatra was the last ruling queen of ancient Egypt, the best-known example of a queen.

clue.text: Scrawny local dressed in the blue

indicators.note: something dressed in clothing is wrapped by it, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a local is a neighbourhood pub, and an inn is a pub
the blue is a poetic phrase for the sky

explanation.surface: A thin resident of the area is dressed all in blue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' looks like a person from the area, but in British usage it is your nearest pub; 'the blue' is the sky, as in 'out of the blue'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a body that is bony and underweight, so they are direct synonyms.

clue.text: Punch highe?

blocks.note: surface reading: a blow aimed upwards, with a typo in the last word
setter's reading: a word meaning loftier with its final letter cut off

explanation.walkthrough: The apparent misprint is the clue: 'higher' (upper) has been cut short, giving an upper cut, which is also a rising boxing blow.
explanation.definitionFit: In boxing, a blow thrown upwards under the opponent's chin is named for its rising path.

clue.text: Worker on plant remarkably green: so true!

indicators.note: something done remarkably is done in an unusual way, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: eleven letters taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone working in a factory is praised as genuinely environmentally minded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as a factory and 'green' as eco-friendly; both really belong to the arboreal world.
explanation.definitionFit: An arborist who prunes and repairs trees works on a large woody form of vegetation.

clue.text: River, black one ebbing in peninsula

indicators.note: an ebbing tide flows back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the Aire is a river in Yorkshire, England
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A dark river flows out to sea on a peninsula.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River' could be R, but the full name of the Aire is needed; all three pieces together then run backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Iberia is the geographical name for the landmass shared by Spain and Portugal, almost surrounded by water.

clue.text: Briton ends in Wales: charabanc to Newport

indicators.note: the ends of words are their final letters, which are the ones kept here

blocks.note: final letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A British traveller's journey ends in Wales, taking a coach to the town of Newport.
explanation.walkthrough: A charabanc is an old-fashioned word for a motor coach used for outings; Newport is a Welsh town, which makes 'ends in Wales' look like geography.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Scotland is a citizen of the United Kingdom, so one kind of Briton.

clue.text: Impressive witness going off

blocks.note: to witness something is to see it, and an eye is what sees, as in eyewitness
going off like a firework or a cork, with a bang

explanation.surface: A star witness leaves the stand having given impressive testimony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going off' suggests leaving, but here it means exploding, as fireworks do.
explanation.definitionFit: Something so striking that it makes your eyes seem to bulge out is spectacular and astonishing.

clue.text: A bore, possible reason for apparent expansion of corporation?

definitions.text: possible reason for apparent expansion of corporation

blocks.note: first meaning: a pompous, dull, self-important person

blocks.clueFragment: possible reason for apparent expansion of corporation
blocks.note: second meaning: a garment packed with padding would make a belly look bigger

explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' sounds like a business, but it is an old jocular word for a pot belly, so a padded garment would make it seem to grow.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a pompous, stuffy person who is tedious company, matching a dull bore.

clue.text: Convention in country adopted by all thieves, literarily?

indicators.note: something adopted is taken into a family, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: Ali Baba's band in the Arabian Nights tale numbered forty thieves
Mali is a West African country

explanation.surface: A nation's custom seems to have been taken up by every criminal in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literarily' points to a book: in 'Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves' the whole gang counts forty, and that number surrounds MALI.
explanation.definitionFit: A formality is an established procedure or custom observed for form's sake, much like a social convention.

clue.text: That woman has welcomed a native of Australia — bravo!

indicators.note: welcoming someone means taking them in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a pronoun for a woman
taken as written
a rhea is a large flightless bird like an emu, though strictly it is South American

explanation.surface: A woman cheers after making an Australian visitor welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird in the middle actually lives in South America; Australia's look-alike is the emu, so the setter's geography is loose here.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are spoken exclamations of approval, the first shouted at performers and the second traditional in debating chambers.

clue.text: Best cricketer, say — spinner?

blocks.note: first meaning: a sportsman who holds a record
second meaning: a turntable machine that rotates discs to play music

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a spinner is a slow bowler who turns the ball, so the surface reads as one cricketer; really the second sense is a gramophone, which rotates vinyl.
explanation.definitionFit: A turntable for vinyl discs revolves as it plays, and a top sportsman holding an all-time best is jokingly named the same.

clue.text: Revolutionary school in London joins a club

blocks.note: Che Guevara, the Latin American revolutionary
the London School of Economics
taken as written

explanation.surface: A radical student from a London college signs up to a society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like an adjective or an indicator to turn something round, but it is the noun: Che Guevara. Chelsea is a London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Chelsea FC is a professional football team based in west London, so it is an example of a club.

clue.text: German discipline evident, having finished off opening German beer

indicators.note: opening something up lets a piece be put inside it, so one goes within the other

blocks.note: Pils is a German lager
having finished off food is having eaten it

explanation.surface: Germanic self-control is on show when someone drains a beer they have just cracked open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finished off' looks like a deletion signal, but it means consumed. Joseph Pilates, inventor of the exercise system, was German.
explanation.definitionFit: This exercise regime was devised by a German, and a fitness method can be called a discipline.

clue.text: Compress fruit

blocks.note: first meaning: to crush or flatten
second meaning: a gourd such as a pumpkin, botanically a fruit

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an instruction to crush fruit, but the verb and the noun are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for pressing flat and a noun for marrows and pumpkins, which botanists class as fruits.

clue.text: Scream with delight about a pop band — decent fare?

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is placed around another

blocks.note: a squeal is a shrill cry of excitement
taken as written
R.E.M., the American rock band

explanation.surface: A fan screams in delight about a pop group and wonders whether the music is any good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' looks like a ticket price or the band's output, but it means food.
explanation.definitionFit: A filling, nourishing meal is idiomatically called square, so it is a decent helping of food.

clue.text: Old sovereign is backing father

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the letters read from the end

blocks.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen
taken as written

explanation.surface: A former monarch is supporting his father's claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' reads as supporting, but it turns the letters round. 'Old sovereign' could also suggest a coin.
explanation.definitionFit: To sire offspring is to beget them, and as a noun it means a male parent, especially of an animal.

clue.text: Beastly sin?

definitions.note: adjective standing for the noun: a beast

blocks.note: first meaning: a slow-moving tree-dwelling animal
second meaning: laziness, one of the seven deadly sins

explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly sin' sounds like a very wicked act, but one word is both an animal and a deadly sin; the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Idleness is listed among the seven deadly sins, and the same name belongs to a slow South American mammal.

clue.text: Bone set briefly, bust in the middle

indicators.note: said briefly, a word is cut short, losing its last letter
the centre of a word is its middle letters, which are the ones kept

blocks.note: a radio set, cut short
the central two letters

explanation.surface: A broken bone is quickly set after a bust-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' looks like a verb for fixing a fracture, but it is a noun: a radio set, then trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: The radius is one of the two long forearm bones, running from elbow to the thumb side of the wrist.

clue.text: Gas ring, note, on the blink

indicators.note: a device on the blink is malfunctioning, so these letters are out of order

blocks.note: eight letters taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone leaves a note that the gas ring on the cooker is broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gas ring' reads as a cooker burner, but the definition stops at 'Gas'; 'ring' belongs to the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitrogen is a colourless chemical element that makes up most of the air, an example of a gas.

clue.text: Sort of heady years, the best period

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant version, so these letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
Y is the abbreviation for years

explanation.surface: Someone recalls rather intoxicating years as the finest time of their life.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost a definition itself, since heady years are a heyday; 'Sort of' is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A heyday is the time of greatest success, popularity or vigour in a person's life or an era.

clue.text: A selection of articles, therefore, for book

indicators.note: a selection is a run picked out of a larger whole, so the letters come from inside the words

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning these two words

explanation.surface: An editor chooses some articles to put together in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests newspaper pieces or grammar words like 'the'; really the letters straddle the end of it and the start of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther is one of the books of the Old Testament, telling of a Jewish queen of Persia.
